b: A behavioral remedy, also called a conduct remedy, is an order from a court or competition authority that tells a company how it must or must not behave, rather than forcing it to sell part of its business. It exists because breaking up a firm is slow, risky and hard to reverse, while many harms flow from specific practices: a contract clause, an auction rule, a refusal to share data. Its opposite is a structural remedy, usually a divestiture.

The term became central to advertising on September 2, 2026, when a federal judge in Virginia rejected the US government's request to force Google to sell its ad exchange, AdX, and accepted "most of the parties' proposed behavioral remedies" instead.

A behavioral remedy arrives after a finding of liability or as part of a settlement. In the US, it takes the form of a final judgment or consent decree entered by a federal court. In the European Union, the Commission imposes it in a decision under Article 7 of Regulation 1/2003, or accepts a company's offer of commitments under Article 9.

The obligations fall into a handful of recurring types. Prohibitions bar a practice, such as exclusive dealing, tying one product to another or favouring an in-house service. Affirmative duties require something new: interoperability with rivals, access to data, non-discriminatory pricing, or disclosure of rule changes. Firewalls separate information flows between business units. Process obligations set up the machinery of enforcement: a compliance officer, regular sworn reports, and often an outside monitor or technical committee with access to code, documents and staff.

Every behavioral decree also has a term. Unlike a sale, conduct rules expire. Six to ten years is common in the US, and courts usually keep jurisdiction to enforce, modify or extend the order. Breaching a decree can be punished as contempt of court.
The Google ad tech judgment shows the anatomy in practice. According to PPC Land's reading of the unsealed 106-page opinion, Judge Leonie Brinkema of the Eastern District of Virginia ordered:

Prohibitions on enforcing any term that ties the DoubleClick for Publishers (DFP) ad server to AdX, on reimposing First Look or Last Look, and on reviving Unified Pricing Rules for indirect transactions. Publishers may again set different floor prices for different buyers.

Interoperability duties, including an interface so that AdX bids can compete inside Prebid, the open-source header bidding framework, and a DFP-to-Prebid connection "functionally equivalent" to the DFP-AdX link. AdX bids must also reach rival publisher ad servers.
A pricing parity rule: AdX's revenue share may not vary according to whether a publisher uses DFP, a rival ad server or Prebid.
Data obligations, limited to open-web display,, with bid-data export and a per-ad data file; video and in-app were left out.
Oversight through a monitor serving for the judgment's full term, a three-member technical committee and an internal compliance officer.
The term is six years, worldwide, from 60 days after entry. Google had asked for six years, the plaintiffs for 15. Display & Video 360 (DV360), Google's demand-side platform, faces no restrictions.

The modern debate over behavioral versus structural relief took shape around Microsoft. On June 7, 2000, Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson ordered Microsoft split in two. The DC Circuit vacated that order on June 28, 2001, and the case ended with a settlement, approved in November 2002, that imposed conduct rules on licensing and interoperability. The last of those provisions expired in May 2011.

The Commission's March 24, 2004 decision against Microsoft fined it EUR 497 million and required interoperability disclosures and a Windows version without Media Player. Enforcement proved difficult: in February 2008 the Commission added a EUR 899 million penalty for non-compliance with the interoperability duty, and in March 2013 it fined Microsoft EUR 561 million for failing to display a browser choice screen it had committed to in 2009.

Regulation 1/2003, applicable from May 2004, wrote a preference into EU law. Article 7 lets the Commission impose "any behavioural or structural remedies which are proportionate", but adds that "structural remedies can only be imposed either where there is no equally effective behavioural remedy or where any equally effective behavioural remedy would be more burdensome for the undertaking concerned than the structural remedy."

US merger policy swung back and forth. The Justice Department's Antitrust Division published a remedies guide in October 2004 and a revised one in June 2011 that was more open to conduct remedies, particularly in vertical deals. The 2011 Comcast-NBCUniversal decree was the emblematic case, with seven years of rules on access to programming. Ticketmaster and Live Nation merged in 2010 under a conduct decree, entered July 30, 2010. In January 2020 a court modified that decree and extended it by five and a half years after the department found violations. "Live Nation broke the promises they made to the court and the American people," said Makan Delrahim, then Assistant Attorney General, according to the department. Under Delrahim the Division withdrew the 2011 guide and, on September 3, 2020, issued a merger remedies manual under which structural remedies are "strongly preferred" and "remedies should not create ongoing government regulation of the market," according to the department's announcement.

Brinkema's April 17, 2025 liability ruling found that Google had monopolised the publisher ad server and ad exchange markets and unlawfully tied DFP to AdX. Because the remedy is behavioral, the fix runs through product changes inside Google rather than a new owner for AdX.

The ruling also leaned heavily on Google's own proposals. A tally by Scott Messer of AdTech Therapy found that all 19 conduct provisions Google drafted appear in the opinion, 16 unchanged and three modified, with the court adding six more. Messer rated four of them as high value for publishers, clustered around rival ad servers, Prebid and the revenue-share rule.

Search marketers live under a parallel decree. On September 2, 2025, Judge Amit Mehta of the District of Columbia rejected a forced sale of the Chrome browser and chose conduct rules: bans on exclusive distribution contracts, data sharing with qualified competitors and disclosure of material changes to ad auctions, for six years. Google filed its appeal on January 16, 2026 against the final judgment of December 5, 2025, and asked the court to pause the data-sharing and syndication remedies.

The case for behavioral remedies is speed, precision and reversibility. Mehta wrote that divestiture should be used "only with great caution" and called a Chrome sale "incredibly messy and highly risky", according to a Congressional Research Service summary. Brinkema found that "structural remedies are neither realistic nor needed," noting that "plaintiffs failed to identify a viable AdX acquirer," and characterised the breakup argument as boiling down to "a lack of trust."

Critics argue that trust is exactly the issue. A conduct decree leaves the incentive behind the original harm in place and asks a monitor to police a firm that knows its own systems far better than any outsider. Economist John Kwoka's 2015 retrospective of US mergers found conduct remedies associated with weaker price outcomes than divestitures, a methodology Federal Trade Commission (FTC) economists have disputed. Live Nation's violations and Microsoft's EU penalties are cited as evidence that compliance is costly to verify. Thomas Höppner of Geradin Partners, who represents complainants against Google, questioned "why the judge concluded behavioural remedies alone will be sufficient."

Time is the other weakness. Rules written for one technology can be overtaken by the next. Implementation can also eat into the term: Karsten Weide of W Media Research said making Google one bidder among many in a Prebid-run auction could see broad adoption only in "2028 or beyond".

There is also a transatlantic split. The European Commission, which fined Google EUR 2.95 billion on September 5, 2025 for favouring AdX, said at the time that "the only way for Google to end its conflict of interest effectively is with a structural remedy," a quote from competition chief Teresa Ribera. Google rejected a breakup in November 2025 and offered behavioral changes.
What a behavioral remedy is not

Structural remedy. A change in ownership, such as selling a business unit or assets. It is a one-off act; a behavioral remedy is an ongoing obligation. Data-access and interoperability duties are sometimes called quasi-structural because they aim to change market structure without a sale.
Commitments. In EU law, Article 9 commitments are offered by the company and made binding without a finding of infringement. Article 7 remedies are imposed after one. Both can be behavioral.
Consent decree. A negotiated court order. It can contain behavioral or structural terms. The Google ad tech judgment is litigated, not consented to.
Behavioral targeting. In advertising, "behavioral" usually means targeting based on browsing history, an unrelated sense.

The parties filed a joint proposed final judgment on October 2, 2026, still disputing whether Google should get six or 12 months to open AdX to rival ad servers. PPC Land coverage reviewed for this article did not report the judgment's entry as of late November 2026. Prebid's proposal to reverse the auction order, so that ad servers including Google Ad Manager bid into a final Prebid auction, went to public consultation after its October 13, 2026 presentation; Weide's assessment of its timeline was published by PPC Land today. In Brussels, Ribera has said the EU "should try to stay consistent with authorities elsewhere," according to Tech Policy Press, and the Commission has adopted no remedy decision in the ad tech case.

Who: Courts and competition authorities impose behavioral remedies; in advertising, the leading examples bind Google under orders from Judge Leonie Brinkema (ad tech) and Judge Amit Mehta (search), with the European Commission still weighing its own remedy.
What: An order that changes a company's conduct, through prohibitions, interoperability and data duties, pricing rules and monitoring, instead of forcing it to sell assets.

When: The approach dates to the earliest antitrust cases, was shaped by the Microsoft cases of 2000 to 2013, and reached ad tech on September 2, 2026, with a six-year term starting 60 days after the final judgment is entered.
Where: In US federal courts through final judgments and consent decrees, and in the EU under Articles 7 and 9 of Regulation 1/2003; the Google ad tech decree applies worldwide.

Why: Behavioral remedies aim to end anticompetitive practices faster and with less disruption than a breakup, but critics argue they leave the underlying incentive intact and depend on monitoring that is hard to make effective.
